title: Recovery-Free CHSH Nonlocality with Particle Loss
abstract: Can CHSH nonlocality survive particle loss without applying an explicit recovery operation? In principle, any deterministic recovery can be absorbed into the measurement. Operationally, we show that the answer depends on the allowed measurements on the lossy system. We distinguish flagged erasure, in which each lost particle leaves a detectable record, from unflagged deletion, in which no such record remains. For flagged erasure and survival probability $η>1/2$, using known quantum-capacity results, we show measurements that asymptotically approach the quantum maximum $2\sqrt2$. In contrast, for $η\le1/2$, CHSH violation is impossible for both loss models. Then, we construct explicit recovery-free protocols using permutation-invariant encodings built from $n$-qubit Dicke states $| D_N^n\rangle$ and measurements on the surviving particles. A one-excitation $(N=1)$ encoding violates CHSH for $η>1/\sqrt{2}$. Increasing the excitation number $N$ yields a family of protocols that violates CHSH for $η>η_G=(\sqrt{5}-1)/2$, with the asymptotic golden ratio approached as $N \to \infty$. Finally, we present a sparse-deletion binomial PI protocol that guarantees CHSH violation for up to $O(\sqrt n)$ deletion errors. Our results distinguish fundamental limits imposed by loss from those set by explicit measurements without recovery.
summary: This work determines the threshold for maintaining quantum nonlocality (CHSH violation) when quantum particles are lost. The authors develop explicit, recovery-free protocols using highly entangled Dicke states to show that nonlocality persists up to specific loss rates $\eta$. This work clarifies the fundamental limits imposed by physical loss channels compared to theoretical measurement constraints.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether quantum nonlocality, quantified by the CHSH inequality, can survive particle loss without requiring an explicit recovery operation.
main_result: The authors construct recovery-free protocols using Dicke states that maintain CHSH violation for loss probabilities $\eta$ exceeding specific thresholds, such as $\eta > \eta_G = (\sqrt{5}-1)/2$ for large $N$.
method: The analysis involves comparing the limits imposed by direct measurements on the lossy state versus those achievable with explicit recovery, utilizing permutation-invariant (PI) encodings.
model_or_system: The system models quantum correlations tested via the CHSH inequality subjected to particle loss, distinguishing between flagged erasure (detectable loss record) and unflagged deletion (no record).
key_observables: The CHSH value $S$, the loss probability $\eta$, and the achievable quantum maximum $2\sqrt{2}$.
important_parameters: Loss thresholds include $\eta > 1/2$ (for flagged erasure) and $\eta > \eta_G = (\sqrt{5}-1)/2$ (for PI protocols).
main_assumptions: The analysis distinguishes fundamental limits imposed by loss from those set by explicit measurements without recovery.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the CHSH violation thresholds for various PI protocols, showing the relationship between the $N=1$ threshold, the large-$n$ limit ($\eta_G$), and the local bound ($S=2$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical bounds for lossy CHSH violation, then constructing explicit recovery-free protocols using low-excitation and general $N$-excitation Dicke states, and finally presenting a sparse-deletion binomial PI protocol.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, constructive framework for testing the robustness of quantum nonlocality against realistic noise channels (particle loss) without relying on idealized recovery operations, which is crucial for experimental quantum communication.
